newsitem.title: USA: Dlr higher at US open on mixed Japanese outlook.
newsitem.headline: Dlr higher at US open on mixed Japanese outlook.

text.p: The dollar was broadly higher at the open Friday after mixed economic data in Japan quelled expectations of a near-term rate hike in that country, analysts said.

Comments from Bundesbank members and European officials added to uncertainty about the single European currency and weighed on the German mark. Strong economic data in Britain boosted sterling/mark to a 59-month high.
At 1230 GMT, the dollar traded at 1.7315/25 marks versus 1.7250/60 at the close Thursday, and at 114.37/47 yen versus 113.10/20.
Japan's industrial output was reported up 3.8 percent in May. But the Trade Ministry also forecast that output would drop 2.6 percent in June and rise a meager 0.9 percent in July.

"The industrial production headline was nice. But, looking forward, it's not so good," said senior currency strategist David Durrand at I.D.E.A. He also noted that the unemployment rate in Japan rose to 3.5 percent in May, its highest level since 1953.
"Any thinking of a rate hike in Japan has to be delayed," Durrand said.
Dollar/yen rose to a high of 114.56 after Japan's industrial output and unemployment data, and held to most of its gains going into the U.S. session.
Meanwhile, Bundesbank Council member Reimut Jochimsen's latest comments on prospects for the single European currency, or Euro, pressured the mark anew.
"There is a sober verdict steadily gaining ground that France is unwilling and Germany unable any longer, at least, to satisfy the (Maastricht debt) criteria," Jochimsen said.
Another Bundesbank council member, Franz-Christoph Zeitler, warned against any deviation from strict Maastricht criteria.

"It would be the wrong way to deviate from a strict and clear fulfillment of the 3.0-percent criterion and open up an upward Richter scale after the decimal point," Zeitler said in a magazine interview.
French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn late Thursday said his country's 1997 budget deficit will be above 3.0 percent, its upper limit under the Maastricht Treaty.
"The key for the Euro is France. The market is telling us we are still looking at a weak Euro and that we have not yet crossed the bridge into the no-Euro," Durrand said.
The mark usually falls on prospects of a weak Euro.
If the planned Euro launch were shelved, the German currency would rally on its regained safe-haven status.
On the German political front, Finance Minister Theo Waigel predicted, "There will be no soft Euro. We will not allow a softening of the Maastricht criteria."
A German magazine also said Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber would vote against the Euro in the German parliament if the Maastricht Treaty criteria were not fulfilled.
The German Constitutional Court has ruled that Germany will not be bound to join the Euro if the Maastricht Treaty is not strictly enforced.
The mark also suffered versus sterling, which was boosted by strong U.K. economic data that continued to point to a tightening in Britain. Sterling/mark surged to a 59-month high.
U.S. economic data were no surprise and had not been expected to be a factor for the dollar on Friday.

The third and final estimate for U.S. first-quarter Gross Domestic Product was an annual growth rate of 5.9 percent, its largest surge in 10 years. Traders said the University of Michigan June index of consumer sentiment was reported at a record high 104.5.
The dollar was quoted at 1.4420/30 Swiss francs versus 1.4355/65 at the close on Thursday, and unchanged at Canadian $1.3818/23.
Meanwhile, cable traded at $1.6662/72 vs. $1.6652/62, and the Australian dollar at $0.7455/60 vs. $0.7495/00.
((--Isabelle Clary, 212-859-1666))
